summary:
Egypt's immigration legislation gives the Ministry of Interior discretion to refuse entry to, or remove, any foreign national held to disturb public order or morality. The Cairo 52 study "Your Kind Is Not Welcome Here" (27 November 2023) reads that statute against the case law built on it and against 12 documented incidents from 2018 to 2022, and finds the power applied to travellers perceived as queer. The Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights records the deportation of foreign nationals suspected of being gay or trans in cases where no charge was ever upheld. Removal requires neither a conviction nor an offence under Egyptian law. The most recent individual removal cases carried in these sources fall inside the 2018 to 2022 window; no later individual case is documented here.

No penal provision names homosexual conduct. Prosecutions proceed instead through Article 9(C) of the Anti-Sex Work Law 10/1961, which the Economic Courts read together with Penal Code provisions. Cairo 52 reported on 24 January 2024 that the Economic Courts have moved from de facto to explicit criminalisation. Court of Cassation interpretations issued in the 1970s had already stripped out the requirement of a financial exchange, so conduct with habitual or multiple partners is enough to sustain a charge. The penalties are custodial: Outright International's country overview, updated 12 March 2026, states that vague public-morality and debauchery provisions are routinely used for arrests that carry prison sentences.

Police build these cases through entrapment on dating apps and websites. A BBC investigation into police use of such platforms describes officers running fake accounts, with victims reporting blackmail and arrest, names changed throughout. The Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights documents the same pattern and identifies transgender women as a particular target of fake-account approaches, and reports that violations continue inside police stations after arrest.

Arrests documented by Bedayaa (February 2023) are accompanied by coerced anal examinations, and the same source states that authorities turn a blind eye to abuses and that Egypt has no anti-discrimination policy or law. Outright International, updated 12 March 2026, confirms the absence of any legal protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression or sex characteristics. Nothing in the inventory supplies a trans-specific violence rate with a population denominator, so no comparative magnitude can be stated.

Gender markers are being closed off. A Ministry of Interior directive issued to civil-registry heads nationwide, reported by Cairo 52 on 12 December 2024, closes the loophole in Civil Status Law 143/1994 that had allowed transgender Egyptians to correct their gender markers through governorate committees. Legal gender recognition is now actively being withdrawn rather than extended, which bears on how the state treats gender status generally.

Access to care is restricted on the same grounds. TIMEP reported on 6 January 2025, for Egypt's fourth UPR cycle, that transgender and intersex Egyptians face discriminatory laws, policies and practices that violate the right to health, that barriers to equitable health services have persisted since the previous cycle, and that discrimination on grounds of gender identity and sexual orientation is pervasive in healthcare provision. A trans visitor requiring medical or emergency care enters that same institutional setting.

Partnership carries no recognition. Personal and family law follows the religious law of the person's recognised religion, Islam or Coptic Orthodox Christianity, and none of those systems recognises same-sex unions, so Egyptian law recognises marriage only between a man and a woman. A trans visitor in a relationship that would be locally classed as same-sex has no recognised status, and if such a relationship becomes public the police may use it as evidence in a criminal indictment under laws against Satanism, prostitution and public immorality.

Expression is also exposed. Morality and public order provisions criminalise any behaviour or the expression of any idea deemed immoral or offensive to religious teachings, which gives police wide latitude over LGBTQ expression. In 2017 the Supreme Media Regulatory Council issued an order barring "the appearance of the homosexuals" or the promotion of their slogans in media, and in August 2018 the government introduced legislation placing any social network user with more than 5,000 followers under increased scrutiny and prosecution under media laws. In 2004 a seventeen-year-old private university student received a 17-year prison sentence, including two years' hard labour, for posting a personal profile on a gay dating site.

State agencies are the documented source of the abuse rather than a protection mechanism. Human Rights Watch documented arbitrary arrests, dark cells and beatings inflicted over sexual orientation during the Queen Boat-era crackdown (29 February 2004), and the record shows police and state officials harassing, abusing and torturing LGBTQ people, particularly trans people, resulting in unfair arrests and abuse in custody. There is no hate-crime regime or statutory aggravation covering anti-trans violence anywhere in this inventory.
tangentialFactors:
The enforcement pattern is long-dated and repetitive. Human Rights Watch's report of 29 February 2004 records arbitrary arrest, detention in dark cells and beatings over sexual orientation, with testimony from defendants. In December 2014 a television presenter collaborated with police on a raid of a public bathhouse that arrested around 26 men, all later acquitted. After the September 2017 rainbow flag incident, two television hosts repeatedly incited violence against the community, one of them publishing personal information of flag-raisers, and at least 84 arrests followed between 25 September and the end of November 2017, many of those arrested subjected to forced anal tests. In January 2019 a television host was jailed for one year for hosting a gay man on his programme. In 2009 a newspaper was shut down and two reporters jailed for printing a story about actors' involvement in homosexual prostitution, and in 2013 a comedian was charged by the Morsi government with propagating homosexuality and obscenity.

These are raw incident counts from a single country's record, not a ranking against other jurisdictions, and the inventory provides no per-capita or comparative denominators for them. The 2017 figures cover a seven-week window in one crackdown and should be read as a documented episode rather than an annual rate.

The September 2017 crackdown is described as producing a state of trauma and despair among young Egyptian LGBTQ individuals, with many attempted suicides; Sarah Hegazi, detained for three months after the incident, fled to Canada, was granted asylum and died by suicide in 2020. Many Egyptian LGBTQ youths left the country under social and political pressure. Bedayaa's February 2023 FAQ documents detention conditions alongside the arrest figures.

Bedaayaa and Outright International both describe an environment in which authorities turn a blind eye to abuses and no anti-discrimination law exists, which places Egypt alongside other states where morality statutes substitute for an explicit prohibition. Unlike jurisdictions that have enacted gender-recognition statutes, Egypt moved in the opposite direction in December 2024 by shutting the administrative route to marker correction.
localsOnly:
Transgender Egyptians lost their administrative route to legal gender recognition when the Ministry of Interior directed civil-registry heads nationwide to close the Civil Status Law 143/1994 loophole that had permitted marker corrections through governorate committees (Cairo 52, 12 December 2024). Residents seeking to align documents with their gender now have no sourced pathway.

Residents face the same arrest machinery described for travellers: fake accounts on LGBTQ dating apps and websites used to entrap individuals, transgender women singled out in that pattern, and violations continuing inside police stations after detention, according to the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights. Bedayaa records rising arrests of homosexual and trans people alongside coerced anal examinations.

Healthcare discrimination is documented as resident-facing and persistent: TIMEP's 6 January 2025 submission for Egypt's fourth UPR cycle reports discriminatory laws, policies and practices affecting the right to health of transgender and intersex Egyptians, with barriers to equitable services unchanged since the previous cycle and pervasive gender-identity and sexual-orientation discrimination in health facilities.

No law or policy prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression or sex characteristics (Outright International, updated 12 March 2026; Bedayaa, February 2023), so residents have no domestic statutory complaint route on those grounds. Personal and family status is settled by the religious law of the person's recognised religion, and no such system recognises same-sex unions.

Media and online expression are regulated for residents: the 2017 Supreme Media Regulatory Council order bars the appearance of homosexuals or the promotion of their slogans in media, and legislation introduced in August 2018 places social network users with more than 5,000 followers under increased scrutiny and prosecution under media laws.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory contains no trans-specific killing or violence figure with a population denominator, so no comparison against Egypt's general homicide rate can be made and none is asserted. It also supplies no raw count of trans victims that could be ranked against other jurisdictions.

No source here documents what happens to a trans traveller at the border itself: whether passport gender markers are inspected, flagged or questioned at ports of entry, whether secondary screening is triggered by marker-and presentation mismatch, or whether a visitor's own documents are treated differently from residents' documents. Those questions are unresolved on this record.

The BBC investigation into police use of dating apps carries no publication date in the inventory, so the recency of that entrapment reporting cannot be fixed. The EIPR and Bedayaa materials likewise give pattern statements without dated individual cases for the most recent period.

The current custodial penalty range under Article 9(C) of the Anti-Sex Work Law 10/1961 is not stated in these sources; the inventory establishes that prison sentences are imposed, not their length, with the exception of the 2004 dating-profile sentence of 17 years and the one-year sentence of January 2019.

Whether the December 2024 Ministry of Interior directive on gender markers has been published in full, challenged in court, or applied uniformly across governorates is not sourced here. Whether removal orders under the immigration provisions can be appealed, and on what timeline, is likewise not covered.
